title: Drinking on a Cruise: Drink Package Math, Seasickness Meds & Safety
excerpt: Is a cruise drink package worth it? How to do the break-even math, how alcohol mixes with seasickness pills and patches, and how to drink at sea without losing days to hangovers.
metaDescription: Is a cruise drink package worth it? Break-even math, seasickness meds and alcohol, BYO rules, and how to drink at sea without losing days to hangovers.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** drinking on a cruise is mostly fine for healthy adults, but three things make it hit harder than a night out at home. Drinks are always within reach (especially with a drink package), you're often in sun and heat all day, and the ship moves, which brings seasickness and seasickness medicine into the picture. Most cruise regrets come from those three, not from the alcohol itself. This guide covers when a drink package actually pays off, how to drink without losing days of your trip to hangovers, how alcohol mixes with seasickness pills and patches, and when to get help from the ship's medical center.

**The quick rules:** Do the package math before you buy, because many people pay for more drinks than they ever have. Pace yourself to about one drink an hour, and drink a glass of water between rounds. Don't mix alcohol with seasickness medicine without checking with a pharmacist first; the labels for the common ones say to avoid alcohol. Respect the sun on pool and beach days. Never sit on or lean over railings after drinking. And if someone is very hard to wake, breathing slowly, or vomiting while barely conscious, call the ship's medical team right away.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article shares general guidance for social drinkers on vacation. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before your trip** if you plan to use seasickness medicine (pills or patches) and drink, take any prescription that warns against alcohol, are pregnant, or have heart, liver, or seizure conditions. **Get help from the ship's medical center right away** if someone can't stay awake, is breathing slowly or irregularly, is confused, has a seizure, has bluish or very pale skin, or vomits while very drowsy. Those can be signs of alcohol poisoning, and it is an emergency.

## Why Drinking on a Cruise Hits Harder Than at Home

A cruise compresses a lot of drinking opportunities into a small, fun space. There's a sail-away party, a pool bar that opens before lunch, wine at dinner, a show, a nightclub, and a casino where drinks keep arriving. None of that is a problem on its own. The trouble is the stacking. Several factors that each make a hangover worse tend to show up together at sea:

- **Long drinking windows.** At home you might have three drinks across an evening. On a sea day, a drink at 11 a.m. can turn into a drink every hour until midnight without anyone really deciding that. The total adds up even if no single moment feels like heavy drinking.
- **Heat and sun.** Caribbean and Mexican itineraries mean hours in strong sun. Alcohol makes you pee more (it suppresses a hormone that normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water), and sweating in the heat drains fluid at the same time. Dehydration doesn't cause every hangover symptom, but it makes headache, dizziness, and fatigue worse.
- **Sweet, strong cocktails.** Frozen drinks and "drink of the day" specials are often large, sugary, and stronger than they taste. Sugar hides the alcohol, so it's easy to drink them quickly.
- **Short, broken sleep.** Late shows, early port arrivals, and a cabin that hums and rocks all chip away at sleep. Alcohol makes sleep lighter in the second half of the night, so you wake up less rested than the hours suggest.
- **Motion.** A moving ship works on your balance system, and so does alcohol. Seasickness and a hangover share nausea, dizziness, and headache, so the two feel worse together.

None of this means you need to skip drinking. It means a cruise is a place where a few simple habits make a big difference to how you feel on day four.

## Is a Cruise Drink Package Worth It? The Math

Drink packages are one of the most searched cruise questions, and for good reason. They're expensive, and the answer depends entirely on how much you'll actually drink. Here's how to work it out for your own trip.

### Step 1: Find the real daily cost

The advertised package price is usually per person, per day. Then the cruise line typically adds an automatic service charge or gratuity on top, often in the high teens as a percentage. Look up both numbers for your line and sailing, and add them together. That's your real daily cost.

Also check these common rules, because they change the math a lot:

- **Every day of the cruise.** Most packages must be bought for the whole sailing, not just sea days. Port days when you're off the ship for eight hours still count.
- **Every adult in the cabin.** Many major lines require all adults in the same stateroom to buy the package if one does. That's meant to stop sharing, but it means a light drinker sharing a cabin with a heavy drinker may pay for drinks they won't have.
- **Daily caps and price limits.** Some packages cap the number of alcoholic drinks per day, or only cover drinks up to a certain menu price. Premium wines and top-shelf spirits may cost extra.
- **What's included.** Some packages bundle specialty coffee, bottled water, and soda. If you'd buy those anyway, that adds real value.

### Step 2: Estimate what you'd pay drink by drink

Look at the ship's bar menu (most lines post it online or in their app) and estimate a typical drink price for what you order. Remember that a gratuity is usually added to individual drink purchases too, so compare like with like.

### Step 3: Divide

**Break-even drinks per day = real daily package cost ÷ typical price per drink.**

Here's an example with round, made-up numbers so you can see how it works. These are not any line's actual prices. If a package costs $80 a day after the service charge, and your usual cocktail costs $14 after gratuity, you'd need to drink about 5.7 cocktails every single day of the cruise to break even. If you mostly drink beer at $9, you'd need about 9 a day.

Now be honest about a typical day. Maybe you'll have two drinks at lunch by the pool, a glass of wine with dinner, and two at the show. That's five. On port days you might have one or two. Averaged across the trip, many social drinkers come in well under the break-even point.

### When a package usually makes sense

- You genuinely drink steadily through the day on a sea-heavy itinerary.
- You'd also buy lots of specialty coffee, smoothies, or bottled water that the package covers.
- You value not tracking a bar tab, and you're okay paying extra for that convenience.

### When pay-as-you-go usually wins

- Your itinerary is port-heavy and you'll be off the ship most days.
- Someone else in your cabin barely drinks but would be required to buy it too.
- You know you tend to drink more when drinks feel "free," and you'd rather not.

That last point is worth taking seriously. A package removes the small pause that paying creates. People often report drinking more on a package simply because it feels wasteful not to. If the main argument for the package is "I'll make sure I get my money's worth," that's a reliable recipe for a rough trip. Pay-as-you-go keeps a natural brake on things.

## Bringing Your Own Alcohol on Board

Policies vary by line and change over time, so always check your cruise line's current rules before packing. That said, the common pattern on major lines looks like this:

- **Wine and champagne.** Many lines allow each adult to carry on a small number of bottles at embarkation. If you open one in a dining room, a corkage fee may apply.
- **Spirits and beer.** Generally not allowed in luggage. If security finds them, they're usually held and returned at the end of the cruise rather than thrown away.
- **Port purchases.** Bottles bought in port or in the ship's duty-free shop are usually held and delivered to your cabin on the last night.

Trying to sneak spirits aboard in disguised containers is a common topic online. It can lead to confiscation and, depending on the line, other consequences. It also tends to backfire in a health sense: drinks you pour yourself in a cabin are often much stronger than a bar pour, and there's no one watching how much you've had.

## The Drinking Age on Cruise Ships

There isn't one global rule. Most cruises leaving from US ports set the minimum drinking age at 21. Some lines allow guests aged 18 to 20 to drink beer and wine on sailings from Europe, South America, or Australia, sometimes only with a parent's written consent. Lines enforce their policy through your cruise card, and breaking it can get a guest's drinking privileges removed or worse. Check your specific line and itinerary.

## Seasickness Medicine and Alcohol: The Part That Matters Most

This is the section people most often skip, and it's the one with real safety stakes. Almost every common seasickness medicine causes drowsiness or fogginess, and alcohol adds to it.

### The common options and what their labels say

- **Dimenhydrinate (original Dramamine).** A sedating antihistamine. The label says to avoid alcoholic drinks while using it, because the drowsiness stacks. We go into detail in our guide to [Dramamine and alcohol](/never-hungover/dramamine-and-alcohol).
- **Meclizine (Bonine, Dramamine Less Drowsy).** Also an antihistamine. It's usually less sedating than dimenhydrinate, but "less drowsy" doesn't mean "not drowsy," and its label also warns against alcohol.
- **Scopolamine patch (sold as Transderm Scop; prescription in the US).** Worn behind the ear and popular with cruisers because one patch lasts up to three days. Its label also advises avoiding alcohol. Scopolamine can cause drowsiness, dry mouth, blurred vision, and, in some people (more often older adults), confusion. Alcohol can make those effects worse.
- **Promethazine (prescription).** A strongly sedating option sometimes prescribed for motion sickness. It should not be combined with alcohol without a doctor's okay.
- **Diphenhydramine (Benadryl).** Sometimes used off-label for motion sickness. It's very sedating and also comes with an alcohol warning. More in our article on [Benadryl and hangovers](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover).

### Why the combination is risky on a ship specifically

Two sedating things together make you sleepier, clumsier, and slower to react than either would alone. On land that's a problem. On a ship it can be more serious, because the floor moves, stairs are steep, decks are wet, and railings are right there. Falls are a real cause of injuries at sea, and some of the most serious cruise accidents involve guests who had been drinking near a rail or balcony.

### A sensible plan

- **Decide before you board.** If you're prone to seasickness and plan to drink, talk to a pharmacist or doctor before the trip. Tell them how you plan to drink, not just that you'll "have a few." They can help you pick the least sedating option and the safest timing.
- **On rough days, choose.** If the sea is rough enough that you need medicine, that's a good day to go light or skip alcohol. Rough seas plus drinks plus sedating pills is the worst version of all three.
- **Don't double up.** Don't take more than the labeled dose because you still feel queasy after drinking. Don't combine two different antihistamines.
- **Watch out for each other.** If a friend took a seasickness pill and has been drinking, they shouldn't be on a balcony alone, in a hot tub, or swimming.

### Drug-free options that help many people

- **Location.** A cabin low and in the middle of the ship moves the least. On deck, look at the horizon.
- **Fresh air and food.** A small, plain snack often helps more than an empty stomach. Crackers and bread are cruise classics for a reason.
- **Ginger.** There's some research suggesting ginger can ease nausea, though results for motion sickness are mixed. It's low-risk for most people. See our look at [ginger for hangovers](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover).
- **Acupressure wristbands.** Evidence is mixed, but they're harmless and some cruisers swear by them.

## How to Drink on a Cruise Without Losing Days to Hangovers

A hangover at home costs you a lazy Sunday. On a cruise, it can cost you a snorkeling trip you paid for. These habits help more than anything else.

### Set a pace, not just a total

Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed rate, roughly one standard drink an hour for many adults, and nothing speeds that up. If you drink faster than that, alcohol builds up in your blood. On a sea day, deciding "one drink an hour at most, and fewer when I'm in the sun" is easier to stick with than a total number for the day. For more on how long alcohol lingers, see [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system).

### Water between every drink

The simplest cruise habit with the biggest payoff: alternate every alcoholic drink with a full glass of water. Water won't cancel out the alcohol, but it slows your pace and helps with the dehydration that sun and alcohol cause together. If plain water gets boring, [coconut water](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) is a common alternative, though it isn't magic either.

### Eat first, and keep eating

Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which means a lower peak and often a gentler morning. Cruise ships make this easy. Have a real meal before the sail-away party, and grab something from the buffet before heading to the evening bars. Our article on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) covers what works best.

### Watch the frozen drinks

Frozen cocktails and tropical punches are often large and sugary, and the sugar hides how strong they are. Some contain more than one shot. You don't have to skip them, but count one big frozen drink as more than one drink, and slow down after it.

### Respect the sun

Alcohol plus hours of strong sun is a common cause of a miserable evening. Drinking can make it easier to fall asleep in a lounger and get badly sunburned. It also adds to fluid loss. On pool days, use shade, reapply sunscreen, and keep a water bottle next to your drink.

### Replace electrolytes after a long day

If you've been sweating in the heat and drinking, an electrolyte drink or oral rehydration packet can help you feel more normal. You don't need anything fancy. Our guide on [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) explains the timing.

### Plan around your excursions

Look at your itinerary and mark any early or active excursions: scuba, ziplining, long hikes, or anything involving boats or heights. Make the night before a lighter one. Many excursion operators won't let a visibly intoxicated guest take part, and diving or swimming with alcohol in your system is genuinely dangerous.

### Protect your sleep

Alcohol helps you fall asleep but makes the second half of the night lighter and more broken. On a cruise, where sleep is already disrupted, that adds up fast. Stopping drinking an hour or two before bed, keeping the cabin cool and dark, and having water by the bed all help. Our guide to [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes deeper on the habits with the best evidence.

## Cruise-Specific Health Issues to Know About

### Stomach bugs

Ships can have outbreaks of norovirus, a contagious stomach virus that causes sudden vomiting and diarrhea. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention runs a Vessel Sanitation Program that inspects ships and tracks outbreaks. The best protection is washing your hands with soap and water, especially before eating, because alcohol-based hand sanitizer works less well against norovirus than it does against many other germs.

This matters for drinking because a stomach bug and a heavy night can look alike at first. If you have vomiting or diarrhea that seems out of proportion to what you drank, keeps going, or other people in your group get it too, tell the medical center. Ships often ask guests to report stomach illness so they can contain it. And if you're already losing fluid from a stomach bug, alcohol will only dehydrate you further, so stop drinking until you've recovered.

### Hangover nausea versus seasickness

Both cause nausea and dizziness, and on a ship it can be hard to tell which is which. A hangover usually peaks in the morning and fades through the day as you eat and rehydrate. Seasickness gets worse when the ship moves more and eases on calm water or on land. Many people have a bit of both. Our guide to [hangover nausea](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers what helps the stomach settle.

### Hot tubs and pools

Alcohol and hot water are a risky pair. Heat widens your blood vessels and alcohol does too, which can make you lightheaded or faint, especially when you stand up. Swimming after drinking raises drowning risk because coordination and judgment drop. Keep drinks out of the hot tub and keep a sober friend around for pool time.

### Railings and balconies

This is the one rule worth repeating: never sit on, stand on, or lean over a railing, especially after drinking. Cruise ship railings are built to a safe height for normal use, and serious accidents are rare, but alcohol is a common factor when they do happen.

## When to See the Ship's Doctor

Most ships have a medical center with a doctor and nurses on call around the clock. Visits cost extra and are often not covered by regular health insurance, which is one reason travel insurance with medical coverage is worth considering. But never let cost delay care in an emergency.

> **Get help right away (call the ship's emergency number or go to the medical center) if someone:**
> - Can't stay awake or can't be woken up
> - Is breathing slowly (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute) or irregularly
> - Is vomiting while very drowsy or passed out (roll them onto their side)
> - Is confused, has a seizure, or has bluish, pale, or cold, clammy skin
> - Fell and hit their head, or has chest pain or a racing heart that won't settle
>
> **See the medical center soon if you have:** vomiting or diarrhea that won't stop, signs of dehydration like very little urine, a dry mouth, or dizziness when standing, a bad sunburn with fever or blisters, or confusion after combining alcohol with seasickness medicine.

Those first signs can mean alcohol poisoning, which is a medical emergency. Don't leave the person to "sleep it off" alone. Stay with them, keep them on their side, and get help.

## Who Should Be Extra Careful

- **People taking seasickness medicine,** sleep aids, anxiety medicine, opioids, or any prescription that warns against alcohol. Talk to a pharmacist before the trip.
- **Older adults,** who tend to feel alcohol and sedating medicines more strongly, and who are at higher risk of falls and confusion with scopolamine.
- **Anyone with heart, liver, or seizure conditions,** or who is pregnant or trying to become pregnant.
- **People doing active excursions** like diving, snorkeling, or ziplining, on the day of the activity and the night before.

## Where Supplements Fit (Honestly)

Some cruisers pack hangover supplements. The most researched ingredient in that category is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that DHM or any supplement prevents a hangover if you drink heavily. It also doesn't change anything about the seasickness-medicine warnings above. Pacing, water, food, and sleep matter far more.

If you want to try it on your trip, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Pack it in your carry-on so it's with you on embarkation day. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and if you take any prescription medicine, check with your pharmacist before adding a supplement.

## The Bottom Line

A cruise is a great place to relax with a drink, and most people do it without any trouble. The difference between a fun trip and a lost one usually comes down to a few decisions: do the drink package math honestly instead of buying it to feel unlimited, pace yourself to around one drink an hour with water in between, eat before you drink, respect the sun, and keep alcohol away from seasickness medicine unless a pharmacist has said your plan is okay. Stay off railings, keep an eye on your friends, and get the ship's medical team involved quickly if someone is very hard to wake or breathing slowly.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is a cruise drink package worth it?**

Only if you will actually drink enough each day to cover the cost. Take the package's daily price, add the service charge the line adds on top, and divide by the average price of the drinks you usually order. If the answer is around six or seven drinks a day and you normally have three, pay as you go. Remember the package usually has to be bought for every day of the cruise, including port days and the day you feel rough, and many lines require every adult in the cabin to buy it.

**Can I take Dramamine or other seasickness pills and drink on a cruise?**

The labels for dimenhydrinate (original Dramamine) and meclizine (Bonine, Dramamine Less Drowsy) tell you to avoid alcoholic drinks, and the scopolamine patch label says the same. All of them can make you drowsy or foggy, and alcohol stacks on top of that. One drink many hours after a single dose is a different risk from cocktails on a rough sea day, but the safest plan is to talk to a pharmacist or doctor before the trip about which option fits how you plan to drink.

**Does alcohol make seasickness worse?**

It can. Alcohol affects the inner ear and balance system, irritates the stomach, and leaves you dehydrated and short on sleep, all of which make motion sickness more likely or harder to shake. A hangover and seasickness also share symptoms like nausea, dizziness, and headache, so they tend to feel worse together. On rough days, eating something plain, staying low and midship, and going easy on drinks usually helps.

**Can you bring your own alcohol on a cruise?**

Usually only in limited amounts. Many major lines let each adult carry on a small amount of wine or champagne at embarkation, sometimes with a corkage fee if you drink it in a restaurant, and they generally confiscate spirits and beer found in luggage and return them at the end of the cruise. Bottles bought in port are usually held until the last night. Rules differ by line and change over time, so check your cruise line's current policy before packing anything.

**What is the drinking age on a cruise ship?**

It depends on the cruise line and where the ship sails. Most cruises leaving from US ports set the minimum at 21. Some lines allow 18 to 20 year olds to drink beer and wine on certain sailings from Europe, South America, or Australia, sometimes with a parent's consent. Check your line's policy for your exact itinerary rather than assuming.

**How do I avoid a hangover on a cruise?**

Pace yourself to roughly one drink an hour or less, alternate every drink with a glass of water, eat before and while you drink, limit sugary frozen cocktails, and keep sun exposure in check on pool days. Plan a lighter night before any early excursion. Some people also use supplements like DHM, but there is no good evidence that any supplement prevents a hangover if you drink heavily; pacing and water matter far more.

**When should someone see the ship's doctor after drinking?**

Go to the ship's medical center, or call for help, if someone can't stay awake, is breathing slowly or irregularly, is vomiting while very drowsy, is confused, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin. Those can be signs of alcohol poisoning. Also get checked for vomiting or diarrhea that won't stop, signs of dehydration like very little urine or dizziness when standing, chest pain, or any fall with a head injury. The medical center charges separately, but don't let cost delay care in an emergency.
